metadata.note: ai-explainer / claude-hai. AI Debt Tracker WEEK 1 — a second reel of a new project, not week 13 of the Private AI Valuation Agent. ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, answered), B09 (verdict artifact), B10 (handoff) and B11 (outro) only — every body beat illustrates its concept as a native animated Remotion scene (REBUILD LAW). The six source PNGs and their SVG sources are REFERENCE in pantry/, never slotted as media. The script's seven sections are split into eight body beats (0:32 splits into B02 design and B03 cut-off) and a limits beat is added; the split is logged in BUILD-LOG.md. FOUR THINGS NOT TO GET WRONG: the agent is NOT built, only the ground under it; 15 rather than 21 is a measurement by coverage, not a recount; 93.4% is on the per-bond quarters and 85% across all of them; and 99% is after six truth corrections on a 29-document set.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about the A I Debt Tracker, a new Mycroft project that follows the bonds and loans paying for the A I build out, and about how I grounded it in real S E C filings before building the agent. The answer key, the cut off that stops it peeking, the matcher and the model are measured. The agent itself is not written yet.

shot.visual_intent: COLD OPEN LAW: the ask is the week itself — ground the project before writing it. Lands ANSWERED.

show.event: The ask types into the Claude composer.
The result lands ANSWERED with three output lines.

props.segment: Grounding an AI Debt Tracker in Real SEC Filings
props.command: New project. Before I write the debt-tracking agent, ground it: build the answer key from real SEC filings, refuse it anything published after the report it is graded on, and tell me what it can actually be graded at.
output: 495 dated test cases across 100 companies, read only up to each cut-off
15 of 25 AI companies can be graded bond by bond — not the 21 I assumed
and the smallest local model read 99% of the bond details, at $0

beats.narration_text: The A I build out is increasingly paid for with borrowed money. In twenty twenty five, the five biggest cloud companies sold a hundred and twenty one billion dollars of U S bonds. Their average over the previous five years was twenty eight billion. Mycroft has agents for news, patents and hiring. None of them watches debt.

shot.visual_intent: One scale, two bars, so 4.3× is seen rather than asserted. The gap is the reason the project exists.

show.event: The 2025 bar grows past the five-year average.
The gap line lands under both bars.

beats.narration_text: The agent will watch S E C filings from twenty five A I companies, read each debt announcement, and keep a ledger of every bond and loan: the amount, the interest rate, the due date. From that ledger it produces a signal. Total debt, new borrowing, and what falls due in the next two years. None of this is built yet.

shot.visual_intent: TENSE DISCIPLINE: a four-box pipeline reads as a description of something that exists, so the frame says in writing that it does not.

show.event: Each box lands in turn, left to right.

beats.narration_text: Each quarter's ledger is graded against that company's next quarterly report, which is published afterwards. So the answer always arrives later than the evidence. A point in time server I did build enforces that: ask it for a filing dated after the report you are being graded on, and it refuses. Without that refusal, every number later in this video would be worthless.

shot.visual_intent: The grading relation is drawn, not implied — the beat is that the answer is published after the evidence.

show.event: A dashed rule descends from the ledger to the later report.
The cut-off rule lands beneath both boxes.

props.sparkLine: The answer always arrives after the evidence.
props.title: Graded against a report it cannot have read
props.ledger: a ledger for the quarter — every bond and loan, with amount, rate and due date
props.answerNote: its debt, machine-readable (XBRL), published after the quarter closes
props.cutoff: Ask it for a filing published after the report you are graded on, and it refuses.
props.whyNote: Without the refusal, every later number in this video is a model that was shown the answer.

beats.narration_text: Before building anything, I asked whether it could fail. On forty six real company quarters, eighty seven and a half percent of new bonds were announced in a filing before the report showed them. And copying last quarter forward is wrong in twenty one of those forty six. So there is something to beat.

shot.visual_intent: Each test carries its OWN pass mark, because the two marks are different numbers and were both set before the test.

show.event: The first bar grows past its own mark.
The second bar lands and the conservative note follows.

props.sparkLine: Could it fail? Two ways, tested first.
props.eyebrow: AI DEBT TRACKER · COULD IT FAIL

props.subtitle: 46 real company-quarters, 23 AI-sector companies

rows.detail: 56 of 64 new bonds, in a filing before the report showed them
21 of 46 quarters changed, confirmed by an announcement

props.legend: dashed = the pass mark, written down before the test ran
props.conservativeNote: 21 of 46 is the conservative count. Raw, carry-forward differed in 33 of 46 — some of that is companies changing how they tag, not new debt.
props.source: SOURCE: AI Debt Tracker docs/feasibility.md · figdata.json

beats.narration_text: Then I built the answer key: every quarterly report since mid twenty twenty four, for the twenty five A I companies and seventy five others. The first surprise was in the tagging. Microsoft's thirteen bonds are really thirteen batches of bonds. Counted by how much of the debt is actually itemised, fifteen companies can be graded bond by bond, not the twenty one I had assumed.

shot.visual_intent: ONE row of 25, partitioned — not three bars. The beat is that a fixed set splits differently once coverage is measured, so the assumption is drawn OVER the measurement.

show.event: The assumed 21 is bracketed first, in outline.
The same 25 fill in beneath it, partitioned three ways.

props.eyebrow: AI DEBT TRACKER · THE ANSWER KEY
props.title: Companies tag their debt more coarsely than they appear to
props.subtitle: 25 AI companies · every quarterly report, Jul 2024 – Sep 2026 · 75 non-AI companies held alongside

segments.note: itemised instruments cover 80%+ of total debt

props.assumedLabel: assumed 21 — counted by tagged members, not by how much of the debt they cover
props.measuredLabel: The same 25 companies, split by how much of each one's debt its report itemises.
examples: Microsoft’s 13 "bonds" are really 13 batches of bonds.
Oracle’s quarterly reports list only the newest few.
props.gateNote: The gate is coverage ≥ 80%. 14 companies qualified outright; one more moved up on a 4–4 tie.

beats.narration_text: So each quarter is graded at the detail its own report gives. That leaves four hundred and ninety five dated test cases: ninety five to build on, and four hundred held back, never tuned on. And on the quarters graded bond by bond, bonds now match from one report to the next ninety three point four percent of the time, above the ninety percent line I set beforehand.

shot.visual_intent: A count broken into its two parts, then ONE gauge — a different object from B05's partition, because this beat is about a split and a score, not a taxonomy.

show.event: The 495 splits into 95 and a held-back 400.
The gauge fills past its pass line.

props.eyebrow: AI DEBT TRACKER · WHAT IT GRADES ON
props.title: Each quarter graded at the detail its own report gives
props.gaugeLabel: Bonds matched from one report to the next
props.caveat: On the per-bond quarters, on the dev split. Across every quarter it is 85% — Intel and Oracle quarters that list few bonds and are graded on totals anyway.

beats.narration_text: Last, the model, on my laptop's eight gigabyte G P U. I gave three local models twenty nine real announcements and no hints, with the rule for picking a winner fixed before the test. The smallest won. Chwen three at four billion parameters read ninety nine percent of the details, in about six seconds a filing, at zero cost. The eight billion version got eighty eight.

shot.visual_intent: ONE shared pass line drawn as a single rule, because one rule was written down and all three models were held to it — unlike B04, where each test had its own mark.

show.at: on 'the rule fixed before the test'
show.event: One dashed rule drops through all three tracks.
The 4B bar overtakes both 8B bars.

Ninety three point four percent is on the per bond quarters; across every quarter it is eighty five. And fifteen rather than twenty one came down to one company on a four four tie.

beats.narration_text: So: the A I build out is being financed with debt, at four times the recent pace, and nothing in Mycroft tracks it. The agent will be graded against the report published after it files, and a server I built refuses it anything later. Four hundred and ninety five dated cases exist, four hundred of them held back. Fifteen companies can be graded bond by bond, not twenty one. And a four billion parameter model on a laptop reads the details better than two eight billion ones, for nothing.

shot.visual_intent: Judgment beat. The artifact page is the point (ILLUSTRATE LAW carve-out).

show.event: Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause.

props.artifactTitle: Grounding an AI Debt Tracker in Real SEC Filings
props.artifactHeading: What week 1 grounded, and what it did not build
artifactLines: $121bn of bonds from 5 cloud companies in 2025, 4.3× their $28bn five-year average — and no Mycroft agent watches debt. That gap is the project.
Every quarter is graded against the company's NEXT report, and the point-in-time server refuses any filing published after it. Built and tested; the agent that keeps the ledger is not.
15 of 25 companies can be graded bond by bond, not the 21 assumed — measured by how much of each company's debt its report itemises, not by counting tags.
495 dated cases, 400 held back and never tuned on. Bonds match report to report 93.4% on the per-bond quarters, against a 90% line set beforehand.
Qwen3 4B read 99% of the bond details in 6.1s a filing at $0, ahead of both 8B models — on 29 documents, after 6 corrections.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Before you build an agent, go and find out what its answer key can actually say. Mine turned out to be coarser than I had assumed, and it changed what the agent is allowed to be graded on. Check before you build, not after.
